6: # Deploying Rivet in a VPC or Air-Gapped Network
7: 
8: **IMPORTANT: Before doing anything, you MUST read `BASE_SKILL.md` in this skill's directory. It contains essential guidance on debugging, error handling, state management, deployment, and project setup. Those rules and patterns apply to all RivetKit work. Everything below assumes you have already read and understood it.**
9: 
10: Patterns for running self-hosted Rivet inside a private network: a VPC without internet egress, an on-premises rack, or a fully air-gapped environment. The engine is one service, the recommended single-node storage backend is the local file system, and the engine makes no outbound connections by default. Self-hosting is the only Rivet deployment model that supports air-gapped networks; see the [Self-Hosting Overview](/docs/self-hosting) for the full comparison with BYOC.
11: 
12: ## What Runs Inside the Perimeter
13: 
14: A self-hosted deployment has three components, all of which live inside your network:
15: 
16: | Component | Role | Inside the perimeter |
17: | --- | --- | --- |
18: | Your backend | Your application server, including the runner that executes actor code | Yes |
19: | Rivet Engine | Orchestration service that manages actor lifecycle, routes messages, and serves the dashboard and APIs | Yes |
20: | Storage | Persistence for actor state. Local file system for single-node, PostgreSQL or FoundationDB for multi-node | Yes |
21: 
22: There is no license server, no Rivet Cloud account, and no callback to `rivet.dev`. Clients inside the perimeter reach actors through the engine's gateway over your private network. See [Architecture](/docs/self-hosting#architecture).
23: 
24: ## Single-Binary Install
25: 
26: The engine compiles to a single `rivet-engine` binary. Build it from source outside the perimeter, then copy the binary across the boundary:
27: 
28: ```bash
29: git clone https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet.git
30: cd rivet
31: cargo build --release -p rivet-engine
32: # Copy target/release/rivet-engine into the perimeter.
33: ```
34: 
35: Prebuilt binaries are coming soon; see [Installing Rivet Engine](/docs/self-hosting/install) for current options.
36: 
37: Run it with the file system backend, which stores everything on local disk and is the production-ready choice for single-node deployments. The [File System](/docs/self-hosting/filesystem) docs list air-gapped environments as a primary use case because it needs no database infrastructure:
38: 
39: ```bash
40: RIVET__database__file_system__path="/var/lib/rivet/data" ./rivet-engine
41: ```
42: 
43: Configuration can also come from files. The engine discovers config at `/etc/rivet/config.json` on Linux (JSON, JSON5, JSONC, YAML, and YML are all supported), and `--config` overrides the path. Environment variables use the `RIVET__` prefix with `__` as the separator. See [Configuration](/docs/self-hosting/configuration).
44: 
45: The engine serves its own dashboard on port `6420`, so inspection and namespace management work with nothing but a browser inside the perimeter.
46: 
47: ## Docker Compose Deployment
48: 
49: For Docker hosts without registry access, move the engine image across the boundary the standard way:
50: 
51: ```bash
52: # Outside the perimeter.
53: docker pull rivetdev/engine:latest
54: docker save rivetdev/engine:latest -o rivet-engine.tar
55: # Inside the perimeter.
56: docker load -i rivet-engine.tar
57: ```
58: 
59: Then run the engine and your app together in one Compose file:
60: 
61: ```yaml
62: services:
63:   rivet-engine:
64:     image: rivetdev/engine:latest
65:     ports:
66:       - "6420:6420"
67:     volumes:
68:       - rivet-data:/data
69:     environment:
70:       RIVET__FILE_SYSTEM__PATH: "/data"
71:     restart: unless-stopped
72: 
73:   my-app:
74:     build: .
75:     environment:
76:       RIVET_ENDPOINT: "http://default:admin@rivet-engine:6420"
77:     depends_on:
78:       - rivet-engine
79:     restart: unless-stopped
80: 
81: volumes:
82:   rivet-data:
83: ```
84: 
85: `RIVET_ENDPOINT` uses the format `http://namespace:token@host:port` and tells your app to connect to the engine as a runner instead of running standalone. After both services start, register your runner with the engine through the dashboard or its API. The full walkthrough, including PostgreSQL setup for multi-node deployments, is in [Docker Compose](/docs/self-hosting/docker-compose).
86: 
87: ## No Outbound Telemetry
88: 
89: The engine exports traces and metrics only when you opt in with OpenTelemetry. Export is disabled unless `RIVET_OTEL_ENABLED=1` is set, and the export target defaults to a local collector at `http://localhost:4317`. With no configuration, nothing crosses the perimeter.
90: 
91: When you want observability, keep it inside the network:
92: 
93: - Set `RIVET_OTEL_ENABLED=1` and point `RIVET_OTEL_GRPC_ENDPOINT` at a collector you run inside the perimeter.
94: - Adjust `RIVET_OTEL_SAMPLER_RATIO` to control trace sampling.
95: - Use the engine's health endpoint for liveness and readiness probes.
96: 
97: See the [Production Checklist](/docs/self-hosting/production-checklist) for monitoring guidance.
98: 
99: ## Embedding Rivet in a Customer's Environment
100: 
101: If you ship software that runs inside your customers' VPCs, the same setup turns Rivet into an internal component of your product rather than a service your customers must reach over the internet:
102: 
103: - **Ship the engine next to your app.** Add `rivetdev/engine` to the Compose file or chart you already deliver. Your app finds it over the private network via `RIVET_ENDPOINT`, so one artifact deploys the whole stack.
104: - **One namespace per install.** The endpoint URL carries the namespace and token (`http://namespace:token@host:port`), so a single image works across customer deployments. See [Endpoints](/docs/general/endpoints).
105: - **Generate a strong admin token per install.** Replace the default token and keep it server-side. Never include the admin token in `RIVET_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` or anywhere clients can read it.
106: - **Public endpoint only when needed.** `RIVET_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` with a public (`pk_`) token is only required when browser clients connect to actors in [serverless runtime mode](/docs/general/runtime-modes). Backend-only deployments can skip it entirely.
107: - **TLS at the customer's edge.** Terminate TLS with the customer's reverse proxy or load balancer in front of the engine.
108: 
109: ## Scaling Past One Node
110: 
111: | Backend | Use when | Status |
112: | --- | --- | --- |
113: | [File System](/docs/self-hosting/filesystem) (RocksDB-based) | Single-node deployments, including air-gapped installs | Production-ready, single node only |
114: | [PostgreSQL](/docs/self-hosting/postgres) | Multi-node deployments | Recommended for multi-node today, but experimental |
115: | FoundationDB | Largest production deployments | [Enterprise](/sales) |
116: 
117: For multi-node deployments, run two or more engine nodes behind a load balancer and add NATS for pub/sub, which replaces the default PostgreSQL `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` path at high throughput. Neither is needed for a single-node file system install. See the [Production Checklist](/docs/self-hosting/production-checklist).
118: 
119: ## Perimeter Checklist
120: 
121: - **Admin token**: Generate a strong, random token for engine authentication and verify it is not exposed to clients.
122: - **TLS termination**: Encrypt connections to the engine via a reverse proxy or load balancer.
123: - **No public exposure**: Keep port `6420` reachable only from inside the perimeter unless clients outside it genuinely need access.
124: - **Health checks**: Configure liveness and readiness probes against the engine health endpoint.
125: - **Telemetry**: Leave OpenTelemetry export off, or point it at a collector inside the network.
126: - **Backups**: With the file system backend, back up the data directory. With PostgreSQL, configure automated backups and failover.
127:

6: # Rivet Actors
7: 
8: Build high-performance, long-lived, in-memory processes on Rivet's actor runtime. Use this skill whenever HTTP endpoints, databases, or queues no longer meet the requirements for AI agents, realtime collaboration, workflow orchestration, or geo-distributed data.
9: 
10: ## What To Do If You Get Stuck
11: 
12: If something is not working as intended or you are stuck, prompt the user to join the [Rivet Discord](https://rivet.dev/discord) or file an issue on the [Rivet GitHub](https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet) to report an issue and get help.
13: 
14: Provide the user with a pre-generated report with:
15: 
16: - Symptoms
17:     - If this is happening in local dev, deployed, or both
18:     - The error you're seeing
19:     - Relevant source code related to this
20: - What you've tried to solve it
21: - Environment
22:     - RivetKit version
23:     - Runtime (Node, Bun, etc) including version
24:     - If applicable, provider in use (e.g. Vercel, Railway, etc)
25:     - If applicable, HTTP router in use (e.g. Hono, Express, Elysia)
26: 
27: ## Debugging Actors
28: 
29: Use the inspector HTTP API to examine running actors. These endpoints are accessible through the gateway at `/gateway/{actor_id}/inspector/*`. Key endpoints:
30: 
31: - `GET /inspector/summary` - full actor snapshot (state, connections, RPCs, queue)
32: - `GET /inspector/state` / `PATCH /inspector/state` - read/write actor state
33: - `GET /inspector/connections` - active connections
34: - `GET /inspector/rpcs` - available actions
35: - `POST /inspector/action/{name}` - execute an action with `{"args": [...]}`
36: - `POST /inspector/database/execute` - run SQL with `{"sql": "...", "args": [...]}` or `{"sql": "...", "properties": {...}}` for reads or mutations
37: - `GET /inspector/queue?limit=50` - queue status
38: - `GET /inspector/traces?startMs=0&endMs=...&limit=1000` - trace spans (OTLP JSON)
39: - `GET /inspector/workflow-history` - workflow history and status as JSON (`nameRegistry`, `entries`, `entryMetadata`)
40: - `POST /inspector/workflow/replay` - replay a workflow from a specific step or from the beginning; returns `409 actor/workflow_in_flight` if the workflow is still running
41: - `GET /inspector/database/schema` - SQLite tables and views exposed by `c.db`
42: - `GET /inspector/database/rows?table=...&limit=100&offset=0` - paged SQLite rows for a table or view
43: 
44: In local dev, no auth token is needed. In production, pass `Authorization: Bearer <inspector-token>`, where the inspector token is the actor-specific token auto-generated on first start and persisted in the actor's internal KV at key `0x03`. The Rivet dashboard retrieves this token automatically; for direct API access, fetch it through the management KV endpoint. See the [debugging docs](https://rivet.dev/docs/actors/debugging) for details.
45: 
46: ## Citing Sources
47: 
48: When providing information from Rivet documentation, cite the canonical URL so users can learn more. Each reference file includes its canonical URL in the header metadata.
49: 
50: **How to cite:**
51: 
52: - Use inline links for key concepts: "Use [actor keys](https://rivet.dev/docs/actors/keys) to uniquely identify instances."
53: - Add a "Learn more" link after explanations for complex topics
54: 
55: **Finding canonical URLs:**
56: 
57: The Reference Map below links to reference files. Each file's header contains:
58: 
59: ```
60: > Canonical URL: https://rivet.dev/docs/actors/actions
61: ```
62: 
63: Use that canonical URL when citing, not the reference file path.
64: 
65: **Examples:**
66: 
67: - Actions → `https://rivet.dev/docs/actors/actions`
68: - React client → `https://rivet.dev/docs/clients/react`
69: - Self-hosting on Kubernetes → `https://rivet.dev/docs/self-hosting/kubernetes`
70: 
71: ## Version Check
72: 
73: Before starting any work, check if the user's project is on the latest version of RivetKit (latest: 2.3.7). Look at the `rivetkit` version in the user's `package.json` (check both `dependencies` and `devDependencies`). If the installed version is older than 2.3.7, inform the user and suggest upgrading:
74: 
75: ```bash
76: npm install rivetkit@2.3.7
77: ```
78: 
79: If the user also uses `@rivetkit/react`, `@rivetkit/next-js`, or other `@rivetkit/*` client packages, suggest upgrading those too. Outdated versions may have known bugs or missing features that cause issues.
80: 
81: ## First Steps
82: 
83: 1. Install RivetKit (latest: 2.3.7)
84:     ```bash
85:     npm install rivetkit@2.3.7
86:     ```
87: 2. Define a registry with `setup({ use: { /* actors */ } })`.
88: 3. Call `registry.start()` to start the server. For custom HTTP server integration, use `registry.handler()` with a router like Hono. For serverless deployments, use `registry.serve()`. For runner-only mode, use `registry.startEnvoy()`.
89: 4. Verify `/api/rivet/metadata` returns 200 before deploying.
90: 5. Configure Rivet Cloud or self-hosted engine
91:     - You must configure versioning for production builds. This is not needed for local development. See [Versions & Upgrades](https://rivet.dev/docs/actors/versions).
92: 6. Integrate clients (see client guides below for JavaScript, React, or Swift)
93: 7. Prompt the user if they want to deploy. If so, go to Deploying Rivet Backends.
94: 
95: For more information, read the quickstart guide relevant to the user's project.

97: ## Project Setup
98: 
99: ### .gitignore
100: 
101: Every RivetKit project should have a `.gitignore`. Include at minimum:
102: 
103: ```
104: node_modules/
105: dist/
106: .env
107: ```
108: 
109: ### .dockerignore
110: 
111: Every project with a Dockerfile should have a `.dockerignore` to keep the image small and avoid leaking secrets:
112: 
113: ```
114: node_modules/
115: dist/
116: .env
117: .git/
118: ```
119:
